title: Daniel
subtitle: Faithful at a foreign court, and visions of kingdoms that end

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Reads the book as history and as prophecy worked out in history. On the traditional dating (Daniel in Babylon and Persia, about 605-530 BC) the stories are events of the exile and the visions foretell Persia, Greece, Rome and what follows. On the late dating (167-164 BC) the stories are older tales told for a later time and the visions of chapters 8 and 11 recount events down to the persecution under Antiochus IV as if they were prophecy. Both readings look at the same kings, wars and dates.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Reads Daniel as a written work with a date, sources, languages and genres (court tale, apocalypse), asking when and why it was made. It weighs the sixth-century case (the Belshazzar evidence, the court details, the Qumran copies) and the Maccabean case (the exact history of chapters 8 and 11, the Greek and Persian words, the apocalyptic form), and notes the middle positions: older tales with a later frame, or a long process of growth. It does not decide for the reader.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Daniel as the rabbis, the medieval commentators and later Jewish scholars do: a book of the Writings, credited to the Men of the Great Assembly (Bava Batra 15a) and read as the story of faithful Jews under foreign rule and as a source for the end of exile, the four kingdoms (the fourth usually Rome) and the Messiah. Traditional Jewish teaching holds the early dating; many modern Jewish scholars date it late, and Jewish writers have always been wary of calculating the end.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Reads Daniel as part of the Christian Old Testament, taking up its themes in Christ: the stone and the kingdom (Daniel 2), the one like a son of man (Daniel 7; Mark 14:62), the resurrection (Daniel 12:2). Hippolytus, Jerome (answering Porphyry's late dating), Calvin and Luther each wrote on it. Christians hold either dating, and many Catholic and Protestant scholars who accept the late date still treat it as Scripture.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Reads parts of Daniel as unfulfilled: the last form of the fourth kingdom, the seventieth seven of chapter 9, the final trouble and the resurrection of chapter 12. This includes the Jewish hope of the Messiah, dispensational futurism (Walvoord) and historicist timelines. On the late dating, the same passages are the author's hope for an end that did not come as expected in 164 BC, and still shape later hopes.

lead: Daniel is a book of two halves. In the first half (chapters 1 to 6) a young Jew, taken from Jerusalem to Babylon, serves at the court of foreign kings with three friends. They refuse the king's food, interpret a king's dream, survive a furnace and a den of lions, and watch two proud kings fall. In the second half (chapters 7 to 12) Daniel himself sees visions: four beasts rising from the sea, a court in heaven, "one like a son of man" given an everlasting kingdom, a ram and a goat, seventy sevens of years, and a long history of two kings that ends with a time of trouble and the rising of the dead.

The book was written in two languages: Hebrew, then Aramaic from 2:4 to 7:28, then Hebrew again. Who wrote it and when is one of the great questions in the study of the Bible. The traditional answer is Daniel himself in the sixth century BC; the answer of most critical scholars is a Jewish writer in 167-164 BC, in the persecution under Antiochus IV. This edition presents both, with their evidence, and does not decide between them. In the Greek Bible the book is longer, with a prayer and a hymn inside the furnace, the story of Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon; Catholic and Orthodox churches count these as Scripture, and this edition treats them as variants and notes.
facts: Not named in the book. Traditionally Daniel, written down in Babylon and Persia; the Talmud says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote it (Bava Batra 15a). Most critical scholars see an unknown Jewish teacher of the second century BC working with older tales.

Traditional: about 605-530 BC (the settings run from Nebuchadnezzar's reign to the third year of Cyrus, 10:1). Critical majority: completed 167-164 BC, with the court tales (1-6) older, perhaps from the Persian or early Greek period. Other views place the stories and the visions in different periods.

The Babylonian court under Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Darius the Mede and Cyrus (chapters 1 to 6 and 10 to 12); the visions of chapters 7 to 9 are dated to Belshazzar's and Darius' reigns. On the late view, the real setting is Judea under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV.
Court tales (1-6) and apocalyptic visions explained by an angel (7-12), with a prayer (9) and hymns. It is the one full apocalypse in the Hebrew Bible.
Hebrew (1:1-2:4a; 8-12) and Aramaic (2:4b-7:28). The Aramaic words in a Hebrew Bible come from Aramaic, not Hebrew: malkuta "kingdom", 'elah "God", qaddishin "holy ones".

12 chapters, 357 verses in English numbering. The Hebrew and Aramaic numbering differs at 4:1-3 (Aramaic 3:31-33) and at 5:31 (Aramaic 6:1). The Greek Daniel adds about 170 verses in the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three, Susanna and Bel and the Dragon.
authorship: Traditional view: Daniel, sixth century BC

The book itself says Daniel was told to "seal up" the book (12:4) and speaks in his own voice in chapters 7 to 12. The Talmud credits the Men of the Great Assembly with writing it down (Bava Batra 15a), and Josephus says the book was shown to Alexander the Great (Antiquities 11.337). Jesus speaks of "the prophet Daniel" (Matthew 24:15). Modern defenders include E. J. Young, Joyce Baldwin, Gleason Archer and Gerhard Hasel. Their points: the book's claims about itself; Daniel's presence at Qumran and in the Old Greek; Belshazzar, whom the Nabonidus Chronicle and the Verse Account show ruling in Babylon as crown prince while Nabonidus was at Teima; the Aramaic, which Kitchen and others place within Imperial Aramaic; and the Persian terms and court detail.

Held from Porphyry (whom Jerome answers) to John Collins, Louis Hartman and Alexander Di Lella, C. L. Seow and Carol Newsom. Their points: chapters 8 and 11 describe events down to 164 BC in detail and then miss (11:40-45 does not match Antiochus' death in Persia); the vagueness about Babylonian and Persian kings ("Darius the Mede"; "Belshazzar the son of Nebuchadnezzar") and the Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242), which tells of a different king's illness; the Greek and Persian loanwords; Sirach 44-50 (about 180 BC) names no Daniel; Daniel stands among the Writings, not the Prophets; and the genre of apocalypse, which grows in the third and second centuries BC. The earliest Qumran copies are dated to the later second century BC (so Ulrich, as reported by Flint), which leaves little time for a book of 164 BC to be copied and spread.

The court tales are older (Persian or early Hellenistic) and the visions are Maccabean (Collins on the stories; a long line of critics). A sixth-century core with Maccabean editing (Goldingay on some chapters). A date in the late Persian or early Hellenistic period (Lucas). Chapters 1 to 6 composed in the third century and the book completed by 164 BC.
If the book is late, is it prediction?

On the late dating, chapters 8 and 11 are history written as prophecy (vaticinium ex eventu), a known form in apocalypses. On the early dating they are real prediction. Each reading can be held without ridicule of the other. Many Catholic scholars (in the period of Pius XII's Divino afflante Spiritu, 1943, and since) and Protestant critical scholars date the book late and still treat it as Scripture; some Jews and Christians hold the early date on traditional grounds.

audience.to: Jews living under foreign rule, in a world of kings who could raise or destroy them. On the traditional view: the exiles in Babylon and Persia in the sixth century BC, whom the stories show how to live at a pagan court and the visions teach that the empires are limited. On the critical view: Jews in Judea and the scattered communities in the Seleucid age, especially the faithful teachers (the maskilim, 11:33-35; 12:3) in the persecution of 167-164 BC.
audience.why: To say that the God of the heavens rules the kingdoms, removes and sets up kings (2:21), and will give an everlasting kingdom to his people. The court tales model a way of living faithfully under a foreign king; the visions tell the faithful that the persecution has a limit and a judge. Knowing it was read by people who might be killed for their faith changes the reading of the furnace and the lions' den, and of the promise of resurrection in chapter 12: they are texts of endurance. The book itself says the vision is "sealed" for a later time (12:4, 9).
views: The stories and visions were first for the Jewish exiles under Babylon and Persia, and kept for the faithful of later generations.

The stories were first told to diaspora Jews as models for life at foreign courts, and the whole was completed for the persecuted of Judea in 167-164 BC; the visions of chapters 8 and 11 were written for the maskilim.
Later readers include the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt, the community at Qumran, the early church facing Rome, the Reformation churches and readers of Revelation.

outline: Four young men taken to Babylon; the food test; ten times better than the magicians
Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the statue; Daniel's hymn; the stone that fills the earth (Aramaic from 2:4)
The golden statue on the plain of Dura and the furnace (the Greek inserts the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three at 3:23-24)
Nebuchadnezzar's tree dream and his madness (English 4:1-3 is Aramaic 3:31-33)
Belshazzar's feast and the writing on the wall
Darius the Mede and Daniel in the lions' den (English 5:31 is Aramaic 6:1; the Greek ends with Bel and the Dragon)
Four beasts from the sea; the Ancient of Days; one like a son of man; the little horn (the Aramaic ends here)
The ram and the goat (Hebrew again)
Daniel's prayer and Gabriel's seventy sevens
The vision by the Tigris; the man in linen
The kings of the south and north down to the contemptible king
The time of trouble, the resurrection, the sealed book

sections.b:
Daniel falls into stories (1 to 6) and visions (7 to 12). The two languages cut across this: Hebrew in 1:1-2:4a, Aramaic in 2:4b-7:28, Hebrew in 8-12. So chapter 7, a vision, belongs with the Aramaic stories, and chapter 1, a story, with the Hebrew visions. A. Lenglet (1972) showed that chapters 2 to 7 form a chiasm, a pattern that reads in toward the center and back out: four kingdoms (2), the furnace (3), the proud king humbled (4), the proud king humbled (5), the lions' den (6), four kingdoms (7). Whether the book was one work by one author or two layers (older tales and a later set of visions) is part of the dating debate below. The Plain marks the switches at 2:4 and 8:1.

English verse numbers differ from the Hebrew and Aramaic in three places: English 4:1-3 is Aramaic 3:31-33 (so English chapter 3 has 30 verses and the Aramaic 33), English 4:4-37 is Aramaic 4:1-34, and English 5:31 is Aramaic 6:1 (so English 6:1-28 is Aramaic 6:2-29). This site uses the English numbers throughout.

sections.h: When and by whom: the whole debate
sections.b:
The facts are agreed; the reading of them is not. The book sets its stories in the sixth century BC. Outside the book, Daniel is called a prophet in Matthew 24:15 and in the Qumran Florilegium (4Q174, on Daniel 12:10); Sirach 44-50, a hymn to famous men written about 180 BC, names no Daniel. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote Daniel down; Josephus (Antiquities 10.11; 11.337) calls him one of the great prophets and says the book was shown to Alexander. In the third century AD Porphyry argued that Daniel was written in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, and Jerome answered him in his commentary of AD 407, which keeps Porphyry's arguments alive.

The fullest cases are in the author lists above. A few points all sides should hear. For the early date: the Belshazzar of the cuneiform sources was a real crown prince acting for his father Nabonidus, and a writer far from the events might not know it; the Aramaic of Daniel is close to the Imperial Aramaic of the Persian period, in the view of Kitchen and Millard. For the late date: chapters 8 and 11 give a detailed sequence of kings that ends with the death of Antiochus (11:40-45) in a way that does not fit what happened, which critics take as the point where the writer's knowledge ran out. Both sides use the same text and the same Qumran copies, the oldest of which are from the late second century BC. This edition's notes state the evidence for each chapter.

sections.h: Daniel the man, and the Daniel of Ezekiel
sections.b: The name means "God is my judge". Ezekiel names a Daniel three times: as one of three righteous men beside Noah and Job (Ezekiel 14:14, 20), and as a figure of proverbial wisdom (Ezekiel 28:3). Is this the hero of the book? Yes, say traditional readers: Daniel was already famous for righteousness and wisdom in Ezekiel's day (about 593-571 BC). No, say others: Ezekiel names Noah and Job, both ancient, and a Danel is the just king in the Ugaritic poem of Aqhat (about the 14th century BC), so the Daniel of Ezekiel is a legendary figure of old, whose name the author of the book gave to his hero (John Day, 1980). Both: a historical Daniel whose name was shaped by the legend. The book says nothing of the matter. It also never says Daniel was a priest or a prophet in his own right; he is a wise man (maskil) and an interpreter.

The book is placed in the age of Babylon's empire. Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC and became king that year; Jehoiakim of Judah was his vassal and then rebelled (2 Kings 24:1). The deportations from Judah came in three main waves: about 605 BC (the tradition behind Daniel 1:1-3), 597 BC with King Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:10-17), and 586 BC at the fall of Jerusalem (some scholars say 587). The Babylonian empire ended in October 539 BC when Cyrus of Persia took the city, as the Babylonian Chronicle and the Cyrus Cylinder show. Belshazzar was the crown prince while Nabonidus lived at Teima in Arabia. The book's "Darius the Mede" is not known outside it (5:31; 6:1; 9:1; 11:1), and who he was is argued (Cyrus himself, a governor named Gubaru or Ugbaru, Astyages, Darius I). The kings' dates in this edition match the site's 2 Kings and Jeremiah and the topic Dating the Kings.

sections.h: Where Daniel sits in the Bible
sections.b: In the Hebrew Bible Daniel is in the Writings (Ketuvim), not the Prophets. Bava Batra 14b lists it between Lamentations and Esther, and printed Hebrew Bibles put it between Esther and Ezra. Maimonides explained why (Guide of the Perplexed 2.45): Daniel speaks of what he saw as a dream and a vision, and the tradition did not count that as the perfect prophecy of the Prophets, so the book was placed among the Writings. In Greek and Latin Bibles, and so in Christian Bibles, Daniel is placed with the Prophets after Ezekiel. Josephus' list of twenty-two books (Against Apion 1.38-41) does not name its books; Josephus elsewhere calls Daniel one of the great prophets (Antiquities 10.11), and the Qumran Florilegium speaks of "Daniel the prophet" (4Q174). The Talmud (Megillah 3a) tells that a heavenly voice stopped Jonathan ben Uzziel from translating the Writings, because they reveal the end; there is no Targum of Daniel in the standard collections.

sections.h: The Greek Daniel and its additions
sections.b: The Greek Daniel exists in two forms. The Old Greek (second century BC) is freer, differs from the Hebrew and Aramaic more than in any other book of the Old Testament, and is known from Papyrus 967 (third century AD) and Codex Chisianus with the Syro-Hexapla. Theodotion, a revision toward the Hebrew, replaced it in the churches; Jerome says that the churches read Theodotion, and the New Testament and Revelation already echo it. Origen's letter to Africanus and Jerome's preface to Daniel discuss the difference. Both Greek forms contain the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three (inserted between 3:23 and 3:24), Susanna (before chapter 1 in the Theodotion manuscripts, after chapter 12 in the Vulgate, and last of all, after Bel and the Dragon, in Papyrus 967) and Bel and the Dragon (after chapter 12). These are the one work Additions to Daniel (deuterocanonical: Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches). This edition follows the Hebrew and Aramaic text and gives each addition as a variant at its place (3:23; 1:1; after 6:28) and in notes; the choice is the same as for the Greek additions to Esther. Which Greek a variant uses is always named.

The rabbis read Daniel as story and as prophecy of the end. They often count the four kingdoms as Babylon, Media, Greece and Edom, that is Rome (Genesis Rabbah 2:4; Leviticus Rabbah 13:5). They tell that the three in the furnace sanctified God's name (Pesachim 53b), debate whether Daniel and his friends were eunuchs (Sanhedrin 93b), and warn against calculating the end (Sanhedrin 97b). Rashi and later commentators wrote on Daniel; their readings of the seventy sevens and the end differ and are given in the chapters concerned.

sections.h: Daniel in the New Testament and the church
sections.b: Jesus speaks of "the abomination of desolation" (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14), the Greek rendering of Daniel's "abomination that desolates" (Daniel 11:31; 12:11). Matthew adds that it was spoken of through the prophet Daniel; those words are not in the oldest manuscripts of Mark. Before the high priest Jesus links the one like a son of man to himself (Mark 14:62; Matthew 26:64). Revelation uses Daniel on almost every page: the four beasts (Revelation 13), the throne room (Revelation 4-5), the time, times and half a time (Revelation 12:14), and the opening phrase "what must soon take place" (Revelation 1:1; Daniel 2:28). Hebrews 11:33-34 alludes to the lions and the furnace. Hippolytus wrote the oldest Christian commentary on Daniel that survives (about AD 204). Jerome's commentary (AD 407) is also the main source for Porphyry's attack. Luther prefaced Daniel in 1530, and Calvin lectured on it.

The Plain translates the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) word by word. The Qumran copies are read in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription: 1QDan-a (1Q71), 1QDan-b (1Q72), 4QDan-a to 4QDan-e (4Q112-4Q116) and 6QpapDan; each variant lists every copy that preserves the place, including those that agree with the Masoretic Text, and never counts a restored word as a scroll's reading. The Greek is read in the Old Greek (Swete's print of Codex Chisianus) and in Theodotion, and each variant says which. The Qumran works that tell stories like Daniel's (the Prayer of Nabonidus, the Aramaic Apocalypse, the Melchizedek scroll) are works, not witnesses to the text, and are named in the notes.

prompts: An ink-and-wash drawing on parchment of the great statue of Nebuchadnezzar's dream: head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, feet of iron mixed with clay, struck by a rough unhewn stone that rolls down from a mountain. Soft, hand-sketched edges, cave-painting texture, Babylonian ziggurat in the background.

A hand-sketched scroll illustration in ochre and charcoal: three men standing unbound in a brick furnace with flames curling around them, a fourth bright figure beside them, and a king peering through the furnace door. Ancient manuscript look with cuneiform-style borders, no hard rectangles.
The beasts and the one like a son of man

A modern-art-meets-cave-drawing image on a scroll: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear, a four-headed leopard, and a terrible beast with iron teeth rising from a stormy sea, and above them a throne of fire with an ancient white-haired figure and a human figure coming on clouds. Soft edges, earth tones.
reading: The standard critical commentary; arguments for the Maccabean date, with the Greek and Qumran evidence.
John E. Goldingay, Daniel, Word Biblical Commentary (1989)
A careful commentary that takes the stories as older than the visions and weighs both datings.
Joyce G. Baldwin, Daniel, Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries (1978)
A short, clear defense of the sixth-century setting.
Carol A. Newsom with Brennan Breed, Daniel, Old Testament Library (2014)
A recent critical commentary with a strong literary eye.
Jerome, Commentary on Daniel (AD 407), trans. Gleason Archer (1958)
The ancient Christian commentary that preserves Porphyry's objections.
The oldest surviving Christian commentary on the book.

traditions.q: Is the Greek Daniel Scripture, with the Prayer of Azariah, the Song of the Three, Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon?
views: Yes. The Council of Trent (1546) received the books of the Old Testament "entire with all their parts" as they stood in the old Latin Vulgate. It does not name the additions to Daniel; they are Scripture because they stood in the Vulgate's Daniel, so the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three (printed as Daniel 3:24-90), Susanna (13) and Bel and the Dragon (14) are Scripture, deuterocanonical. The Song of the Three is sung at Sunday morning prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

Yes. The Orthodox read Daniel in the Greek of the Septuagint tradition, which is Theodotion's text with the additions, and the Song of the Three and the Prayer of Azariah are Odes 7 and 8 of the Matins canon. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672, Decree 4) listed "the history of Susanna" and "the history of the Dragon" with the other deuterocanonical books among the genuine parts of Scripture, though Orthodox teachers also give these books a lower rank.

Not Scripture, but good to read. Luther's Bible printed the additions to Daniel (the Song of the Three, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon) in the section called Apocrypha, a heading that says these are books not held equal to Holy Scripture yet useful and good to read. The Lutheran confessions in the Book of Concord do not list the books of the Bible, so this rests on Luther's Bible and prefaces. His preface to Daniel (1530) is a commentary on the Hebrew book, reading its kingdoms through to Rome and the end.

Not canonical, but read. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lists "The Song of the Three Children", "The Story of Susanna" and "Of Bel and the Dragon" among the books the Church reads for example of life and instruction of manners but does not use to establish any doctrine. The Book of Common Prayer sets the Song of the Three Children as a canticle at Morning Prayer.

No. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture"; the Belgic Confession (article 6) names the Song of the Three Children, Susanna and Bel and the Dragon among the books the church may read for instruction where they agree with Scripture, but not to confirm any point of faith.

No. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) nearly repeats Westminster: the Apocrypha are no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture. Baptist and evangelical Bibles print Daniel as in the Hebrew, without the additions.
